content: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory condition of the airways that affects approximately 334 million individuals globally. During severe asthma exacerbations, patients often require treatment with systemic corticosteroids, which can be administered either intravenously or orally. In some cases, individuals with asthma are prescribed oral corticosteroids (OCS) for self-administration during an exacerbation (referred to as patient-initiated OCS) or for administration by a parent to their child with asthma (referred to as parent-initiated OCS). This method of managing asthma exacerbations is becoming increasingly prevalent. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of patientor parent-initiated oral corticosteroids in managing asthma exacerbations in both adults and children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Airways' Specialised Register (CASR), the US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register (ClinicalTrials.gov), and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The CASR was searched from its inception until May 18, 2016, and the trial registries were searched up to August 24, 2016. No restrictions were placed on the language of publication. The review focused on randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that were either published in full, available as abstracts, or unpublished. Cross-over trials were excluded. The studies included in the review were required to involve adults (aged 18 years or older) or school-aged children (aged 5 years or older) with asthma. Participants needed to be randomised to receive either patientor parent-initiated OCS or a comparator, such as placebo, standard care, an alternative active treatment, or a personalised asthma action plan that did not include the patientor parent-initiated OCS component. Two independent reviewers screened the search results to identify studies that met the inclusion criteria. The primary outcomes of interest were hospital admissions due to asthma, asthma symptoms at follow-up, and serious adverse events. Despite an extensive search of electronic databases and clinical trial registries, no studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. Five studies that appeared potentially relevant were excluded for specific reasons: three studies did not meet the intervention criteria, and two studies employed a cross-over design. Although two of the excluded studies addressed the relevant clinical question, they were excluded because their cross-over design did not align with the review protocol. Attempts were made to contact the authors of the cross-over trials to obtain data from the first treatment period (prior to cross-over), but the data were not available. In conclusion, there is currently no evidence from randomised trials with a non-cross-over design to support or refute the use of patientor parent-initiated oral corticosteroids for managing asthma exacerbations.
